title: FDA clinical decision support: why this app is clinician-facing
summary: Under section 520(o)(1)(E) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, some clinical decision support (CDS) software is excluded from the definition of a medical device. FDA's Clinical Decision Support Software guidance explains four conditions, and software must satisfy all four to be non-device CDS. The current guidance was issued January 6, 2026 and re-issued January 29, 2026, replacing the 2022 version. This app is designed around the four conditions: it is built for licensed clinicians, works from typed symptoms and curated references rather than images or signals, offers suggestions instead of directions, and shows the basis for each suggestion so the clinician can check it independently. This page is information, not legal advice.
keyPoints: First condition: the software does not take in or analyze medical images, signals from in vitro diagnostic devices, or physiological signal patterns such as ECG or EEG waveforms. Software that does is a device no matter what else it does.
Second condition: the software displays, analyzes or prints medical information, such as patient symptoms and history, or published clinical guidelines and studies.

Third condition: the software supports or offers recommendations to a health care professional about prevention, diagnosis or treatment, rather than directing their decision. The 2026 guidance says FDA intends to use enforcement discretion when software gives one recommendation, if only one option is clinically appropriate and the other conditions are satisfied.

Fourth condition: the professional can independently review the basis for each recommendation, so they do not rely mainly on the software. The 2026 guidance moved its discussion of time-critical decisions into this condition.

Patient-facing software is outside this exclusion: software that gives recommendations to patients or caregivers is treated as a device function. That is why client mode shows topics, skills and resources, and never diagnosis names, codes or scores.
FDA updated its general wellness guidance at the same time. Client self-help content should stay general (for example relaxation or sleep habits) and not claim to diagnose or treat a condition.
FDA held a town hall on the final guidance on March 11, 2026. Commentators note the guidance still does not settle every question about documentation tools and AI features.
whatToDo: Treat every suggestion as a starting point for your own assessment, and review the matched and missing features shown with it.
Never show diagnosis suggestions, codes or scores to clients; use client mode for any shared screen or handout.
Report any output that seems to direct care rather than support it, so the owner can correct it.
Owners: re-check the guidance before adding AI, images, wearable signals, time-critical alerts or any patient-facing recommendation.
Consult a regulatory or healthcare attorney before changing the app's intended use; clinicians with practice questions should consult their licensing board.

appPositioning: Clinician mode labels every suggestion For clinician review, shows matched and missing features, uses deterministic and transparent scoring, needs a clinician click to add anything to a plan, and never states a final diagnosis. Client mode shows no diagnosis names, codes or scores. No images or physiological signals are processed, and no AI model is used in Phases 1 to 3.
